The structure: Creative Infrastructure. We help the world catch up to the artist, building lasting ways to encounter the work.

hasPart.name: About our founder
hasPart.text:
Argelys Samuel Oriach is a Dominican-born systems architect, performance artist, and artistic director based in Crown Heights, Brooklyn. He is the founder and artistic director of Wild Lake Studio. He constructs systems and inhabits them. Performance governs his practice, and writing, voice, movement, design, and corporate roles are its forms.

He operates two laboratories: Seven Eighty Three (Lab 783), an independent systems design practice, and Wild Lake Studio, its research laboratory, which guides developing and independent artists. The studio operates from New York, Tampa, and Santiago, and works worldwide.

Wild Lake Studio formalizes Argelys's fifteen-year independent practice. It began in his freshman year at Wesleyan University, when he was initiated into the Eclectic Society and started producing live shows, organizing cultural space, and working alongside artists. Over those fifteen years he has guided twelve or more developing and independent multidisciplinary artists, providing structural stewardship, physical carrying capacity, and live production architecture.

hasPart.name: The Person and the Work
hasPart.text:
Argelys builds infrastructure for artists on the same principles he applies to technical architecture: nothing decorative, and everything carries weight.

He was born in the Dominican Republic to a mother who is a housekeeper and writer and a father who is a facility maintainer and musician. His structural impulse surfaced at eleven, when he taught himself 3D design software to draft his parents' dream home. An architect later used that file for construction. After the 2008 financial crash, he applied to Phillips Academy Andover to design the conditions of his own life on purpose.

A method actor trained in the Alexander Technique, he spent the next sixteen years treating his body, voice, and daily life as a single structural instrument. In 2010 he attended Northwestern University's National High School Institute (Cherubs) theatre program and played Nick in a stage adaptation of The Handmaid's Tale. From there he studied somatic weight, posture, and human attention by inhabiting roles across institutions, physical staging, and corporate infrastructure.

That foundation fueled a twelve-year trajectory building organic growth systems. He served as Cynthia Nixon's social media manager for her 2018 campaign for governor of New York, then moved to architecting sovereign digital frameworks from first principles. He went on to build brand infrastructure at VinePair, direct brand marketing at Kickstarter, and lead organic growth at CookUnity. He approached these corporate roles as an undercover durational performance: a calculated effort to build his life out of poverty while auditing how complex systems scale from the inside out. That cycle recently closed with an intentional return to his body, breath, and voice.

hasPart.name: The Method
hasPart.text: Wild-Lake's method grew through the lived practice described here. The manual sets out how critique, structural honesty, artist wellbeing, and focused interventions operate within an engagement.

hasPart.name: The Creative Practice
hasPart.text:
Performance governs how he works across writing, voice, movement, visual art, design, and acting for stage and screen. “Multidisciplinary” describes the range of media. “Performance artist” describes how he inhabits them.

At Wesleyan he sang with Ebony Singers, studying African-American religious music through performance, including traditional and contemporary gospel, spirituals, and hymns. He also took African drumming courses.

As a writer, he applies the same somatic and structural rigor to narrative in a maximalist, automatic, lyrical, stream-of-consciousness style. His focus remains the physical and digital mechanics beneath every medium.
- This Is Not a Love Story (Yankees): a digital short, published at thisisnotalovestory.net. It is a screenplay written in prose form.
- Graduation: a debut autofiction novel (in progress).
- Untitled One-Act Play (in progress).
- Untitled Pilot (in progress).

hasPart.name: Education
hasPart.text:
He majored in English at Wesleyan University, where he took extensive coursework in studio art and critical theory. His senior thesis was Breaking the circle of the plantation: Violence, affect and the ephemeral in Junot Díaz's Afro-Caribbean literary imagination.

The thesis positions The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao as an alternative archive of the diaspora. It examines Díaz's Afro-Caribbean literary imagination through queer theory, performance studies, affect studies, and critical race theory.

hasPart.name: A personal framework
hasPart.text:
Argelys understands his approach through the architect and shaman archetypes. The architect gives the practice structure. The shaman attends to meaning, transition, and the artist's relationship to their work. Together they make him an alchemist, transforming raw material and lived experience into artistic form. These archetypes inform how he shapes the conditions around an artist while staying close to what the work means to them.

He reflects on his approach through four terms.

Investigation Understanding the foundations before proposing a structure. Asking what is present, what matters, and what the work needs.

Experimentation Learning through making and lived experience. Letting what happens in practice inform the next decision.

Emotional clarity Allowing time to understand a response rather than treating urgency as direction.

Invitation Entering a creative relationship by mutual recognition and consent. Guidance is offered within a relationship the artist chooses.

hasPart.name: Development Protocols | Wild Lake Studio
hasPart.description: Artist wellbeing within a retained engagement: optional practices in reflection, study, grounding, movement, and expression guided by Argelys Samuel Oriach.

hasPart.name: Reflection & Study
hasPart.text: We give the artist space to say what they have been holding, at their own pace. Our attention follows what they choose to share, allowing room for expression before interpretation or revision begins. We expose the load-bearing reality of the artist’s situation, examining what the practice can carry and where its limits are being exceeded. We call this conversational brutalism: applying the architectural principle of exposed structure to information. The conversation makes the conditions visible so the artist can decide what to change and where support is needed. Selected texts give us language for the questions emerging in the practice. Writing continuously lets associations, images, and questions emerge before editing begins. We return to the material afterward to see what it holds. Open conversation generates ideas, associations, and possible directions before we evaluate them. We return to what emerges to identify what the artist wants to explore. Articulating the future the artist wants to build, connecting intention with the choices, resources, and daily conditions that can support it. Gathering images, words, and references into a visual map of creative direction. The board becomes a shared point of reference for priorities and next steps. Images and archetypes provide prompts for interpretation, helping the artist articulate associations, tensions, and possible choices. Attentive listening becomes a study of rhythm, feeling, memory, and how a work holds attention.

hasPart.name: Attention & Grounding
hasPart.text: Steady presence, active listening, and shared attention can support nervous system settling within the working relationship. We agree together on pace, proximity, and boundaries; touch is optional and requires explicit consent. Consent remains ongoing, and the artist can pause, decline, or change direction at any time. Time to notice thoughts, sensations, and the conditions surrounding the work. Gentle attention to breathing and its relationship to movement, voice, and concentration. Self-directed contact can provide a point of physical attention. Any guided touch is discussed and agreed beforehand.

hasPart.name: Movement & Expression
hasPart.text: A change of surroundings can challenge familiar assumptions. Visits may range from a local park or the Blue Ridge Mountains to Santiago and the surrounding campo , where Argelys’s family is rooted. His experience of rural life and poverty grounds conversations about labor, access, and the conditions that sustain a creative practice. The setting and purpose are agreed with the artist. Movement offers a way to explore rhythm, impulse, pleasure, and physical expression. Voluntary movement provides another way to notice and respond to held tension. Emotion can have room without becoming an assignment. Tears, sound, or silence may emerge; none is required as evidence of progress.

hasPart.name: Operational Infrastructure
hasPart.text: We build systems that protect the artist’s attention, income, and direct audience relationships. The tools and boundaries follow the artist’s needs and agreed scope. Route professional inquiries through a structured form on the artist’s domain, using a tool such as Tally or Typeform. Require project scope, a stated budget that meets the artist’s minimum, and acknowledgment of engagement terms before an inquiry reaches the inbox. Close DMs to professional requests and direct cold contacts to the form through saved replies or email autoresponders. Build lightweight sites from portable HTML and CSS, deployed directly to an edge host such as Cloudflare Pages on the artist’s own domain. A simple static site can run without a database, framework, or build pipeline, reducing dependencies and making the work easier to maintain and move between hosts. Replace open calendar booking with an agreed request process. Require a specific agenda at least 48 hours before a proposed call, including the decision needed and relevant material. Book the meeting once its purpose is clear, protecting the artist’s time for independent work. Use payment links such as Stripe Payment Links connected to the artist’s own account, with payouts to their bank account. Send links directly to buyers or place them on the artist’s site, reducing reliance on marketplace commissions. Payment processing fees and the provider’s data handling still apply; the artist controls the offer and customer relationship. Connect a newsletter service such as Buttondown to the artist’s own domain with the required DNS records, alongside an RSS feed on their static site. Build direct subscriber relationships and retain exportable mailing lists and publishing archives, giving audiences ways to follow the work beyond platform algorithms.

hasPart.name: Within an Engagement
hasPart.text: These practices support the artist’s work within an agreed scope. Participation is voluntary, and the artist can pause, decline, or change direction. Each practice returns to a concrete question: what helps this person sustain the work they want to make? Discuss an engagement · The Method

hasPart.name: Your practice is the asset. We find where it is breaking.
hasPart.text: Talent Architecture Your practice is the asset. We find where it is breaking. Talent Architecture is a capacity and boundary audit for creators whose workload has outgrown them. We dismantle the habits that drain you, build an operating framework that protects your autonomy, and step back. You keep your IP, your income, and your decisions.

hasPart.name: Terms of the practice
hasPart.text: Terms of the practice The conditions, the person, and the work. Structural Design How we organize the conditions around the work (time, space, resources, habits, and boundaries) so the practice can sustain what the artist wants to make. Talent Architecture How we develop and support the person carrying the work: their judgment, capacity, autonomy, and relationships. Sovereign A&R How we scout talent and develop creative material through critique, direction, and critical framing. The artist retains ownership and creative control.

hasPart.name: The structural principle
hasPart.text: The structural principle Nature is brutalist. Nothing in it is decorative, and everything carries weight. We build infrastructure for artists under that same principle. Clients come to Wild-Lake to build a practice, or when the way they work has become unsustainable. The engagement is a controlled demolition, undertaken with the artist. We take the practice down to its studs, remove the habits and brittle systems that can no longer carry the work, and rebuild around what the artist needs to operate with clarity. We dismantle the architecture of extraction. The artist leaves the loop intact.

hasPart.name: Critique & revision
hasPart.text: Critique & revision Development requires close study of the material and direct revision with the artist. Critique is the primary mechanism of care. We examine the work closely enough to offer an interpretation the artist can use as scaffolding or tear down. Sustaining the work also means managing the creator's own internal engine. The practice confronts the ego patterns and self-referential loops that drain creative stamina. We help the artist stop depending on outside validation and build grounded autonomy. That protects the person and, through the person, the work. Stewardship spans mediums: visual art, sculpture, installation, short stories, plays, scripts, essays, songs, films, and performance. It also covers the macro-systems that keep those practices standing over the long term. Audience development is part of that infrastructure. We build publishing channels and lasting relationships with the people who encounter the work, and the creator sets the terms of engagement.

hasPart.name: Structural honesty
hasPart.text: Structural honesty We expose the load-bearing reality of the artist's situation: what the practice can carry, and where its limits are exceeded. We call this conversational brutalism, the architectural principle of exposed structure applied to information. The conversation makes the conditions visible so the artist can decide what to change and where support is needed.

hasPart.name: Observation & absence
hasPart.text: Observation & absence We come close only to observe and edit, and to bring clarity to the raw material. Then we depart. The response, the execution, and the timeline remain the artist's. We build for asynchronous stamina. Engagements alternate between high-density structural interventions and extended absence, which gives the artist the isolation to execute without surveillance.

hasPart.name: Artist wellbeing
hasPart.text: Artist wellbeing During a retained engagement, Argelys may guide practices that bring attention to the artist's habits, physical experience, and creative direction. We support artists healing from narcissistic abuse, examining narcissistic patterns within themselves, or both. The work centers on rebuilding self-trust, recognizing harmful relational patterns, and setting boundaries that protect creative autonomy. Building a sustainable practice can include healing from trauma and seeing how past experience shapes the conditions of making. We make room for that history when setting the pace, boundaries, and expectations of an engagement. The artist decides what to share. Our role is to support the practice, with room for care beyond the studio. Explore the practices Development Protocols Active listening, structural honesty, automatic writing, grounding, movement, and vision quests, alongside operational systems for inquiries, communication, payments, and direct publishing. Each practice is optional. The artist can pause, decline, or change direction. Explore the protocols →

hasPart.name: Institutional stewardship
hasPart.text: Institutional stewardship We work with curators as a buffer between the artist and institutional demands. Together we examine what an engagement asks of the artist, set boundaries around access and output, and address pressures that could exhaust the person sustaining the work. As artist developers, our role is to make those boundaries hold.

hasPart.name: Ownership & engagement
hasPart.text: Ownership & engagement The artist retains ownership and creative control. We scout talent and work with artists directly, or partner with record labels, galleries, and booking agencies. Either way, the artist enters the engagement willingly, on their own initiative or through a representative. The Stewardship Subscription reserves availability between client-triggered interventions. Response times, scope, and capacity are agreed in advance. Fixed project commissions and focused advisory engagements are also available. Engagement formats and fees · Terms of Practice

hasPart.name: Retainer terms.
hasPart.text: Focused intervention. Space to execute. The monthly Stewardship Subscription keeps studio capacity available between interventions. We come close to observe and edit, then step away while the artist executes on their own timeline. Wild-Lake takes no percentage of artist earnings or ownership of their intellectual property. The client retains ownership of their work. The Studio retains its proprietary frameworks and licenses delivered framework materials for the client’s practice. Public-facing writing transfers to the client upon final settlement. The client triggers an intervention when it is needed. We agree response times, reserved capacity, and the scope of each intervention in advance. Periods of absence are part of the engagement, giving the artist room to work independently. Their consent and creative control remain explicit throughout. The subscription is paid monthly in advance for reserved availability across the agreed cadence. Project commissions carry a fixed fee.
